opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly the answer has been shifting quite a lot over the last couple of years. For a long time, the default was that almost all of the compute went into pre-training. You'd build this enormous model by predicting the next token over basically the whole internet, and then post-training, the fine-tuning and RLHF, was a relatively thin layer on top. Inference was just the cost of serving it.

What's changed is that we've discovered reinforcement learning, especially on problems where you can verify the answer, like math or code, scales much better than people expected. If you let the model try things, get a signal on whether it was right, and learn from that, you keep getting improvements. So the RL portion is no longer a small polishing step. It's becoming a real fraction of the total budget, and I think it'll keep growing.

Then there's inference. Once models can think before they answer, generating a long chain of reasoning, trying different approaches, checking their work, you get this new axis where spending more compute at test time gives you a better answer. That's quite profound, because it means capability isn't fixed when training ends. You can trade compute for quality per query.

So how should it be divided? I don't think there's a fixed ratio. These three things are complementary. Pre-training gives you the base knowledge and the priors; without a strong base model, RL doesn't have much to work with, because the model has to sometimes stumble on the right answer to learn from it. RL teaches the model how to use that knowledge, how to reason and pursue a goal over many steps. And inference compute lets it apply that reasoning to the specific problem in front of it.

I'd say we're moving from a world that was maybe ninety-plus percent pre-training to something more balanced, where RL and inference each take a meaningful share. And there's a nice feedback loop: the reasoning traces from inference can become training data, which makes the next model better. The boundaries between the three start to blur.

The practical answer is that you should keep measuring where the next unit of compute buys you the most capability, and that marginal return keeps moving. Right now a lot of the low-hanging fruit seems to be in RL and test-time thinking, but I wouldn't count pre-training out. Every time people say it's plateauing, someone finds a better data mix or a better architecture.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reinforcement learning for verifiable math and code, but does not identify AlphaGo self-play as consuming most of its compute.

r002.rationale: It describes a shift toward a more balanced allocation, but does not propose that pre-training receive roughly half of compute.

r003.rationale: It says RL should receive a meaningful share and notes its potential, but does not propose allocating most post-pre-training compute to RL when good rewards are available.

r004.rationale: It discusses spending more inference compute for better answers, but does not mention scientific tasks such as protein folding or justify much longer inference times for them.

r005.rationale: It describes inference as receiving a meaningful share in a more balanced allocation, not as a small fraction of training compute.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is a question we debate constantly, and I'll say upfront that the honest answer is: nobody knows exactly, and the ratio keeps moving.

If you go back a few years, it was essentially all pre-training. You'd spend 99 percent of your compute on the big run, and then fine-tuning and RL were a rounding error on top. That made sense because pre-training scaling laws were so clean. You put in more data and more FLOPs, and loss goes down in a predictable way. It was a very comfortable regime to be in.

What's changed is that we've found other axes that also scale, and they're not fully redundant with pre-training. RL, especially with verifiable rewards, teaches the model things that are hard to get from next-token prediction alone. Things like actually finishing a long chain of reasoning, checking its own work, using tools, and recovering from mistakes. And inference-time compute, letting the model think longer, is another lever that compounds with both of those. The interesting thing is that these three are coupled. A better pre-trained model makes RL more sample-efficient. Good RL makes each inference token more valuable. So it's less a pie you divide and more a system you tune.

My rough intuition for where things are heading is that pre-training stays very important but becomes a smaller fraction of total spend, maybe something like a plurality rather than a near-monopoly. RL grows substantially, because the gradient per FLOP there still looks steep, and we're nowhere near saturating it. And inference becomes a huge chunk, perhaps the biggest over the lifetime of a model, simply because once the model is useful, the world runs it billions of times.

There's one subtlety I'd emphasize, though. Inference compute isn't only a deployment cost. It's also a training signal. The traces you generate when the model thinks hard become the data for the next round of RL, and even feed back into pre-training corpora. So the boundaries are blurring. In some sense you're taking the compute you would have spent on raw data at the start and spending it later, on the model generating and verifying its own experience.

So if you forced me to give a number for today, I'd say something like a rough balance between pre-training and post-training, with inference on top dwarfing both over time. But I'd put very low confidence on the exact split. The thing I'm more confident about is the direction: compute is moving later in the pipeline, closer to the point where the model is actually doing the task.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention AlphaGo or say that self-play reinforcement learning consumed most of its compute.

r002.rationale: It describes pre-training as a plurality and suggests a rough balance between pre-training and post-training, but does not clearly propose that pre-training account for roughly half of total language-model compute.

r003.rationale: It says reinforcement learning will grow substantially, but does not propose allocating most compute remaining after pre-training to RL or make that allocation conditional on having good rewards.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss scientific tasks, protein folding, or using longer inference times for difficult queries.

r005.rationale: The response says inference may become a huge chunk and dwarf training over time, the opposite of proposing it as a small fraction of training compute.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think there’s a fixed ratio. You have to ask: for the next unit of compute, where do you get the biggest improvement? And that depends on the model and what you want it to do.

Pre-training gives you a very broad foundation. Reinforcement learning can help turn that foundation into better problem-solving behavior. Then inference gives you the ability to spend more computation on a particular problem. If a question is easy, you probably want an immediate answer. If it’s a difficult mathematical problem, you might be happy to let the system work for much longer.

Those investments also interact. Spending more on reinforcement learning might teach the model to use its inference budget more effectively. So I wouldn’t optimize the three independently.

There’s an economic question, too: training is an upfront cost, whereas inference is a cost you pay every time someone uses the model. The right balance for a system answering billions of queries could be quite different from one working on a small number of very valuable scientific problems. I’d expect the allocation to keep changing as we learn what scales.

r001.rationale: The response does not identify AlphaGo self-play or say that it consumed most of AlphaGo’s compute.

r002.rationale: It gives no proposed share of compute for pre-training.

r003.rationale: It says reinforcement learning can improve problem-solving and interact with inference, but does not propose spending most post-pre-training compute on it when good rewards are available.

r004.rationale: It says difficult math problems may warrant longer inference and contrasts valuable scientific work with billions of queries, but does not clearly state that difficult scientific tasks such as protein folding justify much longer inference than ordinary queries.

r005.rationale: It does not propose that inference compute should be a small fraction of training compute; it says the balance depends on use and will change.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of it as a joint optimization problem. You have compute you can spend during pre-training to build a strong starting point, compute you can spend on reinforcement learning to improve how the model solves problems, and then compute at inference time to let it work longer on a particular problem.

The right allocation depends on what you’re trying to do. If you’re going to answer billions of relatively simple queries, spending more during training may make sense because you amortize that cost. If you’re trying to solve a very difficult problem, you may be willing to spend much more at inference time.

And these things interact. For additional inference compute to be useful, the model needs to know how to use it. So I wouldn’t expect a fixed percentage for each bucket. The interesting question is where the next unit of compute gives you the biggest improvement, and that balance will keep changing.
